rationale: The chosen topology is an inductively-degenerated common-source amplifier with a tapped inductive load, optimized for low-noise performance at 2.44 GHz with stringent S11 and Idd constraints. This structure achieves excellent input matching through the series inductor (Lg) and gate degeneration, while the tapped inductor (Ld) provides a high-Q resonant output load that enhances gain and noise figure. The use of a series inductor at the gate enables a low-noise design without relying on large resistive degeneration, and the tapped inductor allows for impedance transformation that supports the required 50 Ω input match while maintaining high gain. The topology is well-suited to the 45nm CMOS process, where parasitic capacitances are significant and inductive tuning is essential for narrowband performance. It avoids floating nodes, respects the device budget (3–16), and uses inductors within the allowed range (L_min = 300 pH, L_max = 12 nH), fulfilling the inductorless-rejection constraint. The architecture is inherently robust to gate-to-drain feedback due to the low forward admittance of the degenerated CS stage, and the output stage is isolated from the input by the inductor, avoiding the match-forbidden zone issue. This design leverages the playbooks: it avoids input matching failure by not relying solely on gate degeneration (preempting the "gate-driven-input-is-quiet-only-when-unmatched" pitfall), maintains swing efficiency without over-funding the output stage (avoiding "split-budget-starves-the-swing-stage"), and uses the inductor to open the match front-side without relying on cascode isolation (respecting "match-forbidden-zone-is-architectural").
